cards.method: Ensemble forecast combination (equal / in-sample / CV weights)
cards.when: a robust combination of 2-7 univariate models (a/e/f/n/s/t/z) on ONE series; a baseline macro forecast where stability matters
cards.when_not: multivariate/structural analysis (VAR/VECM), causal Granger, a need for statistically exact PI, or a single dominant model; length(y)<4

alternatives.alt: a single model (#7 automatic ARIMA/ETS, or #8)
alternatives.criterion: one model clearly dominates or you want interpretable parameters/diagnostics
there are cross-series dependencies/cointegration that the univariate combination ignores
you want a posterior-weighted combination with full uncertainty quantification

output_key_fields: included_models: which components ACTUALLY took part after the automatic removals
dropped_models: requested but NOT included (length removal or a drop by hybridModel) — always check it
weights_method / weights: the method + per-model weights (summing to ~1)
point_forecast: ts -> {values,start,frequency}, the central forecast
lower / upper: matrix h x length(level) -> nested rows+dim+axis labels, the PI bounds
pi_combination: 'extreme' (the more extreme bounds) or 'mean'
pi_disclaimer: an explicit statement that the PI are over-conservative
interpretation_traps: the PI are OVER-CONSERVATIVE: lower/upper are heuristic, with no guaranteed nominal coverage — not strict statistical bounds
silent degradation: hybridModel removes components on its own (STL/neural-net if length<2*frequency, ets if the seasonal period>24) — read dropped_models/included_models
neural-net (n) is stochastic (random initial weights): the wrapper enforces a local seed (default 42L); changing the seed changes the forecasts
in-sample errors are not recommended as weights: they overfit; equal weights are more robust, and cross-validated errors are better but slow and data-hungry
the weights reflect low error, NOT the structural correctness of the component (a purely predictive criterion)
sources: Bates & Granger 1969 The Combination of Forecasts
Timmermann 2006 Forecast Combinations (Handbook of Economic Forecasting)
Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice

cards.method: Online probabilistic forecast combination via CRPS-Learning (BOA/BEWA/ML-Poly/EWA aggregation of quantile expert forecasts)
cards.when: you have >=2 experts producing PROBABILISTIC (quantile) forecasts at the SAME tau levels and you want to combine them ADAPTIVELY online (the weights are learned sequentially from the past loss), optimally under CRPS; experts = a 3D array [T x quantiles(P) x experts(K)], y = a Tx1 realized series; appropriate when the relative performance of the experts changes over time (regime shifts) and you want per-quantile weights + the out-of-sample loss against each expert
cards.when_not: point-only forecasts rather than quantiles -> #85; hierarchical or temporal RECONCILIATION rather than combination -> reconcile_cross_temporal / reconcile_grouped; a single expert (K<2, so there is nothing to combine); batch or offline optimal fixed weights rather than online adaptivity (outside the curated surface); you simply want to EVALUATE a density forecast rather than combine -> #94 sr_crps_sample

alternatives.criterion: point-forecast combination (not probabilistic/quantile) over a single ts
hierarchical/temporal RECONCILIATION (coherence within a hierarchy) rather than learning weights from a loss
reconciliation over keyed series (#209), with MinT, WLS or OLS weights
you want ONLY the evaluation of a density/quantile forecast (CRPS/LogS/PIT), not a combination

output_key_fields: predictions: a T x P matrix, the combined probabilistic forecast per time and quantile level (chart data; sorted when allow_quantile_crossing=False)

final_weights: a P x K matrix (the adaptive weights at the last instant T+1; the weights with which the experts will be combined in the NEXT forecast; they sum to ~1 per quantile for method boa/bewa/ewa)
mean_weights: a P x K matrix (the average weight over time per expert × quantile — which expert dominated overall)
forecaster_loss_total / forecaster_loss_mean / forecaster_loss_per_quantile: the cumulative & mean CRPS-learning loss of the COMBINATION (per quantile, of length P)
expert_loss_total: a length-K cumulative loss for EACH single expert (the baseline); best_expert = the best single one
beats_best_expert: True when forecaster_loss_total <= min(expert_loss_total) — the combination beats the best single expert out of sample, which is the reason online learning exists
interpretation_traps: dims: experts MUST be [T x P x K] with dim1==length(y), dim2==length(tau); the wrong axis order (e.g. [T x K x P]) passes silently and gives a WRONG result -> a hard gate checks dim2==length(tau); double-check that the 2nd dimension is quantiles (in the same order as tau)

tau must be STRICTLY increasing & must match exactly the quantile levels at which the expert forecasts were computed; a mismatch -> an invalid loss (the gate blocks values outside (0,1)/unsorted values but NOT a semantic mismatch of levels — that is the caller's responsibility)

method: 'bewa' (default) = the BOA regret + an EWA weight update; 'boa' = the full BOA (second order); 'ewa' = plain exponential weighting; 'ml_poly'; different adaptivity — 'ewa'/'ml_poly' may not give simplex weights with thresholds
beats_best_expert=False is NOT a failure: with a small T, or one dominant expert, online learning needs time to converge; look at mean_weights — is it learning the right expert? — before rejecting it
allow_quantile_crossing=False (the default) sorts the predictions per t, giving monotone quantiles; True allows crossing and hence an invalid CDF — leave it False for interpretable quantiles
smoothing (a B-spline/P-spline across quantiles) is NOT exposed (the defaults mean no smoothing); for smooth per-quantile weights you need a custom fit outside the node
predict/update (incremental on new data) are NOT exposed: a stateless node -> every call is a complete re-fit over the supplied window
sources: Berrisch, J. & Ziel, F. (2023) CRPS Learning, Journal of Econometrics 237(2):105221 <doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2021.11.008>
Gaillard, P. & Goude, Y. (2015) Forecasting electricity consumption by aggregating experts (BOA/ML-Poly online aggregation)
Wintenberger, O. (2017) Optimal learning with Bernstein Online Aggregation, Machine Learning 106:119
precondition_tools: c02_univariate_forecasting/grouped_arima_ets.run_grouped_arima (it produces the quantile forecasts of one expert; repeat per model and stack them into a [T x P x K] array)
c02_univariate_forecasting/grouped_arima_ets.run_grouped_ets (a second expert for the array; at least two are needed)

cards.method: Coherent forecast reconciliation (cross-sectional / temporal / cross-temporal) via an optimal least-squares projection (MinT: ols/str/wls/shr/sam)
cards.when: you have INCOHERENT base forecasts of a linearly constrained (hierarchical/grouped) multiple series — e.g. GDP = the sum of sectors, national = the sum of regions, or annual = the sum of quarters — and you want to make them COHERENT (the aggregates equal the sum of the components exactly) while ALSO improving accuracy through MinT (Wickramasuriya 2019). type: 'cs' a cross-sectional hierarchy, 'te' temporal (one series, several frequencies), 'ct' cross-temporal (both at once)
cards.when_not: a single series with no hierarchical or temporal constraint structure (there is nothing to reconcile); you want to COMBINE alternative forecasts of the SAME series, an ensemble or model average (-> #85, or the combination of #209); you do not have base forecasts for ALL the levels of the hierarchy; you want probabilistic or bootstrap reconciled paths (outside the curated surface)

alternatives.criterion: MinT shrinkage (Wickramasuriya 2019) — the normal default for accuracy when you have in-sample residuals; ols/str ignore the error covariance
you want simultaneous cross-sectional AND temporal coherence (e.g. quarterly regional series summing to an annual national total)
you want a COMBINATION of several models for ONE series (an ensemble), not the reconciliation of a hierarchy
the reconciled forecasts must be non-negative (e.g. counts, positive magnitudes)

output_key_fields: reconciled: the coherent forecasts — cs, an (h x n) matrix; te, a vector of length h*(k*+m) with labels; ct, an (n x h*(k*+m)) matrix (chart-data)
type/comb/approach/nn: the reconciliation that was performed
cs: n/n_upper/n_bottom/h + coherence_err (max|upper - agg_mat·bottom| ~0 => coherent, a post-check)
te/ct: agg_order/m/kt/h + tew; ct: n/n_upper/n_bottom
object: the foreco object (fitted)
interpretation_traps: the ORDER OF THE base COLUMNS/ROWS: cs columns = [upper.., bottom..] (the n_a upper series FIRST, then the n_b bottom ones) consistent with agg_mat; the wrong order => a silently wrong reconciliation (the wrapper checks ONLY the dimension n, not the semantic mapping)
comb DIFFERS by type: 'wlsv' is valid only for te/ct (NOT cs); 'oasd' only for cs; the wrapper blocks an invalid comb for a given type
MinT (shr/wls/sam/acov..) REQUIRES res (the in-sample residuals); without res -> a gate stop; ols/str/csstr/testr do NOT need res
temporal base ordering: LOW->HIGH frequency (the most aggregated first, e.g. annual, then semi-annual, then quarterly); the wrong order => a wrong result
a scalar agg_order m => ALL the divisors of m are used (k*+m = the sum of the divisors; m=4 -> 7, m=12 -> 28); length(base) must be a multiple of that
reconciliation is NOT an ensemble: it combines forecasts of DIFFERENT series/frequencies within one hierarchy so that they add up; it does NOT average models of the same series
sources: Wickramasuriya, S.L., Athanasopoulos, G. & Hyndman, R.J. (2019), Optimal forecast reconciliation through trace minimization (MinT), JASA 114(526):804-819. doi:10.1080/01621459.2018.1448825
Hyndman, R.J., Ahmed, R.A., Athanasopoulos, G. & Shang, H.L. (2011), Optimal combination forecasts for hierarchical time series, CSDA 55(9):2579-2589. doi:10.1016/j.csda.2011.03.006
Athanasopoulos, G., Hyndman, R.J., Kourentzes, N. & Petropoulos, F. (2017), Forecasting with temporal hierarchies, EJOR 262(1):60-74. doi:10.1016/j.ejor.2017.02.046

Di Fonzo, T. & Girolimetto, D. (2023), Cross-temporal forecast reconciliation: Optimal combination method and heuristic alternatives, Int. J. Forecasting 39(1):39-57. doi:10.1016/j.ijforecast.2021.08.004
Panagiotelis, A., Athanasopoulos, G., Gamakumara, P. & Hyndman, R.J. (2021), Forecast reconciliation: A geometric view, Int. J. Forecasting 37(1):343-359. doi:10.1016/j.ijforecast.2020.06.004
precondition_tools: c02_univariate_forecasting/grouped_arima_ets.run_grouped_arima (it produces the base forecasts per series and level; stack them into a base matrix or vector)
c02_univariate_forecasting/classical_univariate_forecasting.run_ets (an alternative producer of the base forecasts and residuals for the MinT combination)
reconcile_cross_temporal (an ols baseline first; then MinT shr/wls with res for accuracy)

cards.method: Tidy hierarchical/grouped forecast reconciliation (aggregate_key + MinT/bottom_up) in the long-format forecasting framework
cards.when: you have a long panel (an index + >=1 key/grouping columns + a numeric value) that aggregates naturally into a hierarchy (e.g. region/sector -> national, or CPI sub-indices -> the headline) and you want COHERENT forecasts — the leaves must sum EXACTLY to the aggregates; one base model (ARIMA/ETS/SNAIVE) is fitted per node and reconciled with MinT (min_trace) or bottom_up
cards.when_not: a single univariate series with no hierarchy (-> #85, or a standalone ARIMA); you want an online adaptive combination of experts (-> #207); purely cross-temporal reconciliation of numeric matrices with no keyed table (-> #208); a value with a gap, or an irregular index; structural or causal analysis (VAR/VECM)

alternatives.criterion: you want cross-sectional, temporal or cross-temporal reconciliation of READY base forecasts as numeric matrices, not a keyed-table round trip
ONE series without a hierarchy — you want an ensemble of several models rather than a coherent hierarchy
a single node / no need for coherence — a plain ARIMA/ETS fit + forecast
you want a posterior-weighted combination with full uncertainty quantification rather than a MinT projection

output_key_fields: reconciled: data_frame records (the key columns + index + point + lower_L/upper_L per level) — the COHERENT forecast (chart-data); aggregated nodes are labelled '<aggregated>'
base: the corresponding records of the UNRECONCILED base forecasts (to compare the effect of the reconciliation)
hierarchy: a data_frame of the hierarchy nodes (each row = a key combination; '<aggregated>' = an aggregated level); n_series (leaves+aggregates); n_leaf
method / reconciliation: the selected method (min_trace(<method>) or bottom_up); structure (nested/grouped); base_model
object: the reconciled model table — stubbed by to_mcp, since nothing downstream in the category consumes it
interpretation_traps: coherence != accuracy: reconciliation GUARANTEES that the leaves sum to the aggregates, NOT that every node becomes more accurate — MinT (min_trace) typically improves matters, but bottom_up can worsen the top level if the leaves are noisy

choosing the MinT method: 'wls_struct' (default) = structural scaling, always robust; 'mint_shrink' (Wickramasuriya 2019) = shrinkage towards a diagonal, theoretically optimal but it NEEDS enough residuals — with short/few series it can be unstable; 'ols' ignores scale
'<aggregated>' in the key fields = an aggregated level (is_aggregated), NOT a category literally named '<aggregated>' — do not read it as a leaf

nested (grp1/grp2) vs grouped (grp1*grp2): nested => a genuine hierarchy (a region within a state); grouped => crossed without natural nesting (e.g. purpose x state) — the wrong choice changes which nodes exist

the PI come from the reconciled predictive distribution (hilo) — valid intervals per node, but the joint coherence concerns the points (the means), it does not guarantee joint coverage of the intervals
the value must aggregate meaningfully (a flow/stock): the coherence constraint is the sum of the leaves = the aggregate; ratios/percentages/index levels do NOT add up -> do not use them as the value
sources: Wickramasuriya, Athanasopoulos & Hyndman 2019 JASA 114(526) (optimal forecast reconciliation through trace minimization)
Wickramasuriya, Athanasopoulos & Hyndman (2019) Optimal forecast reconciliation for hierarchical and grouped time series through trace minimization, JASA 114(526):804
Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice (3rd ed.), ch. 11 Forecasting hierarchical and grouped series (https://otexts.com/fpp3/hierarchical.html)
Hyndman, Ahmed, Athanasopoulos & Shang (2011) Optimal combination forecasts for hierarchical time series, CSDA 55:2579
precondition_tools: reconcile_grouped (run it with method='bottom_up' as a coherence baseline before comparing with MinT)
c02_univariate_forecasting/grouped_arima_ets.run_grouped_arima (checking the base model on a single node before the hierarchy)

cards.when: several forecasts exist and combining them almost always beats selecting one
cards.when_not: one forecast dominates on every fold; the weight-estimation sample is too short and equal weights will do better

alternatives.criterion: the forecast combination puzzle: hard to beat
weight by past accuracy, no estimation of covariances
estimated weights, optionally constrained

output_key_fields: weights: the combination weights
combined: the combined forecast
improvement: accuracy against the best individual and against equal weights
method: which weighting produced them
interpretation_traps: THE FORECAST COMBINATION PUZZLE IS REAL: equal weights frequently beat estimated optimal weights out of sample, because estimating weights adds more variance than it removes bias
unconstrained regression weights can be negative or exceed one, which is legitimate but fragile; constraining them usually improves out-of-sample performance
weights estimated on the same data used to evaluate the combination overstate its benefit
sources: Bates & Granger 1969 (Operational Research Quarterly 20:451-468)
Granger & Ramanathan 1984 (Journal of Forecasting 3:197)
Smith & Wallis 2009 (Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics 71:331)
statsmodels

cards.method: Density combination: linear and logarithmic opinion pools
cards.when: combining predictive DISTRIBUTIONS rather than points, where the pooling rule changes the shape of the answer
cards.when_not: the forecasts are points; the component densities are not on a common support

alternatives.criterion: a mixture: can be multimodal and is wider than its components
a geometric mean: unimodal and narrower
weights update on predictive performance

output_key_fields: combined_density: the pooled predictive distribution
weights: the pooling weights
pool_type: linear or logarithmic, which determines the shape
log_score: of the pool against its components
interpretation_traps: A LINEAR POOL IS ALWAYS AT LEAST AS DISPERSED AS ITS COMPONENTS and can be multimodal; a logarithmic pool is narrower and unimodal -- the choice is substantive, not technical
linear pools are typically underconfident, which is why they are often recalibrated afterwards
weights based on the log score are dominated by the component that avoided the worst outcome, not the one that was best on average
sources: Hall & Mitchell 2007 (International Journal of Forecasting 23:1-13)
Geweke & Amisano 2011 (International Journal of Forecasting 27:465)
Genest & Zidek 1986 (Statistical Science 1:114)

cards.method: Dynamic model averaging and dynamic model selection
cards.when: which model is best changes over time, and the combination should track that instead of averaging over the whole sample
cards.when_not: the best model is stable; the model space is too large for the recursion to be feasible

alternatives.criterion: the ranking is stable
weights evolve with performance
you want the single best model at each date

output_key_fields: weights: the time path of model probabilities
combined: the averaged forecast
selected: the highest-probability model at each date
forgetting: the forgetting factors used
interpretation_traps: THE FORGETTING FACTORS CONTROL EVERYTHING: close to one gives a nearly static average, lower values chase noise -- and the results move a great deal between them
the model space grows exponentially in the number of predictors, so the approach is feasible only with a restricted set
dynamic model selection is far more volatile than averaging and frequently forecasts worse despite picking the best model ex post
sources: Raftery, Karny & Ettler 2010 (Technometrics 52:52-66)
Koop & Korobilis 2012 (International Economic Review 53:867)

cards.when: learning how to combine forecasts from their cross-validated errors, rather than from a fixed rule
cards.when_not: the cross-validation folds are too few for the meta-learner to be estimated; the components are near-identical

alternatives.criterion: few components, stable
you want learned weights with some structure
the best combination depends on the state

output_key_fields: meta_model: the fitted combination rule
weights: implied component weights, where the meta-learner is linear
cv_predictions: the out-of-fold predictions the meta-learner was trained on
improvement: against equal weights and the best component
interpretation_traps: THE META-LEARNER MUST BE TRAINED ON OUT-OF-FOLD PREDICTIONS; training it on in-sample fits leaks and produces weights that collapse onto the most overfitted component
the folds must respect time order for time-series data, or the combination learns from the future
a nonlinear meta-learner needs far more folds than a linear one and usually overfits with typical macro sample sizes
sources: Wolpert 1992 (Neural Networks 5:241-259)
Breiman 1996 (Machine Learning 24:49)
sktime

cards.when: forecasts made at different frequencies for the same series disagree, and reconciling across the temporal hierarchy improves all of them
cards.when_not: there is a single frequency; the series cannot be aggregated to higher levels meaningfully

alternatives.criterion: one frequency only
aggregate, forecast and combine
full temporal-hierarchy reconciliation

output_key_fields: reconciled: forecasts coherent across every aggregation level
levels: the temporal aggregation levels used
weights: the reconciliation weights
improvement: accuracy per level against unreconciled forecasts
interpretation_traps: TEMPORAL AGGREGATION CHANGES THE APPARENT DYNAMICS: a series can look noisy monthly and strongly trending annually, which is exactly the information this method exploits
reconciliation guarantees coherence, not accuracy -- forecasts can be made coherent and worse if the covariance is badly estimated
the aggregation levels must divide the seasonal period evenly or the hierarchy is not well defined
sources: Athanasopoulos, Hyndman, Kourentzes & Petropoulos 2017 (European Journal of Operational Research 262:60-74)
Kourentzes, Petropoulos & Trapero 2014 (International Journal of Forecasting 30:291)
hierarchicalforecast

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: Handle to a long-format DataFrame (index column + >=1 key columns + numeric value column).

arguments.name: index
arguments.description: Time column name (valid series index: Date/yearmonth/yearquarter/numeric).

arguments.name: keys
arguments.description: Key/grouping column names (>=1; they define the hierarchy's nodes); grouped requires >=2.

arguments.name: value
arguments.description: Measured numeric column name (without NA; summed into the aggregates).

arguments.name: structure
arguments.description: Structure: nested (grp1/grp2 hierarchy) or grouped (grp1*grp2 crossed; default nested).

arguments.name: base_model
arguments.description: Base model per node (ARIMA/ETS/SNAIVE; default arima).

arguments.name: method
arguments.description: Reconciliation: min_trace(method) MinT variants or bottom_up (default wls_struct — robust structural MinT).

arguments.name: h
arguments.description: Forecast horizon (positive integer; default 8).

arguments.name: type
arguments.description: Reconciliation framework: 'cs' cross-sectional (csrec; agg_mat), 'te' temporal (terec; agg_order), 'ct' cross-temporal (ctrec; agg_mat+agg_order).

arguments.name: base
arguments.description: Handle to the base forecasts. cs: (h x n) matrix, columns [upper..., bottom...] (n=n_a+n_b). te: (h*(k*+m)) vector lowest->highest freq. ct: (n x h*(k*+m)) matrix.

arguments.name: agg_mat
arguments.description: Handle to the (n_a x n_b) aggregation matrix (map bottom->upper). Required for type='cs' and 'ct'.

arguments.name: agg_order
arguments.description: Max temporal aggregation m (e.g. 4 quarterly->annual, 12 monthly) or a vector of factors of m. Required for 'te'/'ct'.

arguments.name: comb
arguments.description: Covariance/MinT method (closed set PER type). cs: ols/str/wls/shr/oasd/sam. te: ols/str/wlsh/wlsv/acov/strar1/sar1/har1/shr/sam. ct: ols/str/csstr/testr/wlsh/wlsv/acov/bdshr/bdsam/Sshr/Ssam/shr/sam/hbshr/hbsam/bshr/bsam/hshr/hsam. WLS/GLS/MinT require 'res'. Default 'ols'.

arguments.name: tew
arguments.description: Type of temporal aggregation (te/ct): sum/avg/first/last (default sum).

arguments.name: approach
arguments.description: Approach: proj(ection)/strc(structural)/*_osqp (default proj).

arguments.name: res
arguments.description: Handle to in-sample residuals/validation errors (required for WLS/GLS/MinT comb). cs: (N x n) matrix. te: (N*(k*+m)) vector. ct: (n x N*(k*+m)) matrix.

arguments.name: nn
arguments.description: Non-negativity algorithm for reconciled forecasts (default 'none').

arguments.name: y
arguments.description: Handle to a Tx1 matrix of realized values (probabilistic setting); without NA.

arguments.name: experts
arguments.description: Handle to a numeric 3D array [T x quantiles(P) x experts(K)]: experts[t,,k] = quantile forecasts of expert k at the tau levels; dim1==length(y), dim2==length(tau), K>=2, without NA.

arguments.name: tau
arguments.description: Probability levels in (0,1); STRICTLY increasing/unique; length P == dim(experts)[2].

arguments.name: method
arguments.description: Online-learning algorithm (default bewa· boa=full BOA, ewa=exp. weighting, ml_poly=ML-Poly).

arguments.name: loss_function
arguments.description: Loss (default quantile = pinball/CRPS scoring).

arguments.name: loss_parameter
arguments.description: Scaling of the loss power (> 0; default 1).

arguments.name: loss_gradient
arguments.description: Linearized (gradient) version of the loss (default True).

arguments.name: lead_time
arguments.description: Offset of expert forecasts (0 = t+1 at t); integer 0<=·<T.

arguments.name: forget_regret
arguments.description: Share of past regret to forget per iteration; in [0,1] (default 0).

arguments.name: fixed_share
arguments.description: Fixed share added to the weights; in [0,1] (1 => uniform; default 0).

arguments.name: gamma
arguments.description: Scaling of the learning rate (> 0; default 1).

arguments.name: soft_threshold
arguments.description: Soft-threshold on the weights (default -Inf = none).

arguments.name: hard_threshold
arguments.description: Hard-threshold on the weights (default -Inf = none).

arguments.name: allow_quantile_crossing
arguments.description: False => the forecasts are sorted ascending per t (default False).

arguments.name: seed
arguments.description: Seed (integer >=0) — determinism of any grid sampling.

arguments.name: y
arguments.description: Handle to a univariate ts/numeric series to forecast.

arguments.name: models
arguments.description: String of component-model letters (>=2 distinct): a=auto-ARIMA e=ETS f=theta n=neural-net s=STL t=TBATS z=seasonal-naive (default 'aefnst').

arguments.name: weights
arguments.description: Combination weighting method (default equal).

arguments.name: errorMethod
arguments.description: Error metric for the weights (when weights != equal; default RMSE).

arguments.name: h
arguments.description: Forecast horizon (positive integer); default 2*frequency if seasonal, otherwise 10.

arguments.name: PI_combination
arguments.description: How the components' prediction intervals are combined (default extreme; the PI are OVER-CONSERVATIVE, non-nominal coverage).

arguments.name: cvHorizon
arguments.description: CV horizon (only weights='cv.errors'; default frequency(y)).

arguments.name: windowSize
arguments.description: CV window length (only weights='cv.errors'; default 84).

arguments.name: seed
arguments.description: Seed for DETERMINISM (neural-net's 'n' is stochastic; default 42).

arguments.name: actual
arguments.description: Realised values.

arguments.name: forecasts
arguments.description: Forecasts, one column per method.

arguments.name: method
arguments.description: Weighting method.

arguments.name: window
arguments.description: Rolling window for the weights; omitted = expanding.

arguments.name: constrain
arguments.description: Constrain weights to be non-negative and sum to one.

arguments.name: densities

arguments.name: pool
